meta.title_en: The Sifted Treatise on Legal Theory

chapters.title_en: The Sifted Treatise on Legal Theory — Section 1: The Preeminence of Jurisprudence and the Threefold Division of the Religious Sciences
chapters.arabic_text:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
الحمد لله رب العالمين والصلاة والسلام على محمد نبيه وعلى آله وصحبه
أجمعين
قد تقرر عند ذوي الألباب أن الفقه أشرف العلوم وأعلاها قدرا وأعظمها خطرا
إذ به تعرف الأحكام ويتميز الحلال عن الحرام وهو على علو قدره وتفاقم أمره
في حكم الفرع المتشعب عن علم الأصول ولا مطمع في الإحاطة بالفرع وتقريره
والاطلاع على حقيقته إلا بعد تمهيد الأصل وإتقانه إذ مثار التخبط في الفروع
ينتج عن التخبط في الأصول ولتعلم أن علوم الشرع ثلاثة الكلام والأصول
والفقه
ولكل واحد منها مادة منها استمداده وإليها استناده ومقصود به يتعلق قصد
الطالب وارتياده فلابد من التنبيه على مادته ليقتبس الخائض فيه منها مبلغ
حاجته فيتوسل إلى بغيته ولا غنى عن التنبيه على مقصوده لئلا يكون الطالب
على عماية من مطلبه فأما علم الكلام فمادته الميز بين البراهين والاغاليط
والميز بين العلوم والاعتقادات والميز بين مجاري العقول ومواقفها وأما
مقصوده فهو الإحاطة بحدوث العالم وافتقاره إلى صانع مؤثر
متصف بما يجب من الصفات منزه عما يستحيل تخيله صفة للذات قادر على بعثة
الرسل وتأييدهم بالمعجزات وأما الأصول فمادته الكلام والفقه واللغة ووجه
استمداده من الكلام أن الإحاطة بالأدلة المنصوبة على الأحكام مبناها على
تقبل الشرائع وتصديق الرسل ولا مطمع فيه إلا بعد العلم بالمرسل ووجه
استمداده من الفقه أنه المدلول وطلب الدليل مع الذهول عن المدلول مما تأباه
مسالك العقول ووجه استمداده من اللغة كون الأصولي مدفوعا إلى الكلام في
فحوى الخطاب وتأويل أخبار الرسول عليه السلام ونصوص الكتاب ومقصوده معرفة
الأدلة القطعية المنصوبة على الأحكام التكليفية وأخبار الآحاد ومسالك العبر
والمقاييس والمستثارة قال بطرق الاجتهاد ليس من
الأصول فإنها مظنونات بجانب أخذها مأخذ القطعيات ولكن افتقر
الأصولي إلى ذكرها لتبين الصحيح من الفاسد والمستند من الحائد ولأن
الترجيحات من مغمضات علم الأصول ولا سبيل إليها إلا ببيان المراتب والدرجات
وأما الفقه فمادته الأصول ومقصوده معرفة الأحكام الشرعية وتقرير الأحكام
عند ظهور العلامات المظنونة معلومة بأدلة قطعية  لا ظن فيها

### | فصل

ما من علم من هذه العلوم إلا وله مواقع إجماع ومثارات نزاع فمطلع الإجماع
في الكلام المدركات بالبداية والضروريات والمعقولات التي يتحد
فيها صوب النظر ولا يتعدد كإجماع العقلاء على أن القديم لا يعدم ومثار
الخلاف فيه تعارض الأدلة والشبهات وأما علم الأصول فمنشأ الوفاق فيه يضاهي
منشأ الوفاق في الكلام ومنبع الخلاف فيه أمران أحدهما تعارض الأدلة
والشبهات والثاني امتزاج القطع فيها بالظنيات وأما الفقه فموضع الإجماع فيه
ما يستند إلى نص كتاب الله أو حديث متواتر أو إجماع واجب الإتباع وما عداها
فهو من مظان الظنون وعند الإرتباك فيها يختلف المجتهدون وتضطرب آراؤهم
فيتحزبون
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ق-ه (fa-qāf-hā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Comprehensive understanding (al-fahm al-dāqq); in the technical sense, knowledge of the rulings of the Law derived from their specific evidences.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The perception of the inner meaning of a thing (idrāk al-shayʾ ʿalā maʿnāhu al-bāṭin); applied to the science of revealed rulings (ʿilm al-aḥkām al-sharʿiyyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — deep comprehension; metaphorical (majāz) — the technical legal science built upon it.
- Root: أ-ص-ل (alif-ṣād-lām)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root/base of a thing (asās al-shayʾ); that upon which something is built and to which it returns.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The foundational principle (al-qāʿidah al-umm) from which branches (furūʿ) derive; in uṣūl al-fiqh, the evidences of the Law in their totality.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the lower base of a wall; metaphorical — the epistemic foundation of a discipline.
- Root: ك-ل-م (kāf-lām-mīm)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Speech (al-nuṭq); the act of speaking (al-takallum).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The science of Kalām — discourse concerning the divine attributes and the proofs of the faith (al-baḥth ʿan al-ṣifāt wa-ithbāt al-ʿaqāʾid bil-adillah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — articulated speech; metaphorical — the theological science that defends the creed through rational demonstration.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — When the author lists the three sciences (al-kalām, al-uṣūl, al-fiqh) and then elaborates each with "fa-ammā... fa-māddatuhu," the anaphoric structure (al-takrār al-maqṣūd) serves to disambiguate the referent of each pronoun, preventing iḥtimal (ambiguity) in the periodic sentence.
chapters.translation:
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace be upon Muhammad, His Prophet, and upon his family and his Companions, all of them.

It has been established in the minds of those possessed of intellects (ulū al-albāb) that jurisprudence (al-fiqh) is the noblest of the sciences, the highest of them in rank, and the greatest of them in gravity — for through it the rulings are known, and the lawful is distinguished from the unlawful. Yet despite the loftiness of its rank and the magnitude of its affair, it stands in the position of a branch (farʿ) ramifying from the science of the principles (uṣūl). And there is no aspiration to encompass the branch, to establish it firmly, or to gain insight into its true reality, except after the root (aṣl) has been prepared and perfected — for the source of confusion in the branches is generated by confusion in the roots.

Know that the religious sciences are three: theology (al-kalām), the principles of jurisprudence (al-uṣūl), and jurisprudence (al-fiqh). Each one of them has a material (māddah) from which it derives and upon which it leans, and a purpose (maqṣūd) to which the aspiration of the seeker and his pursuit are attached. It is therefore necessary to draw attention to its material, so that the one who plunges into it may kindle from it the measure of his need, and thereby attain his quest. Nor is there any dispensation from drawing attention to its purpose, lest the seeker remain in blindness concerning that which he seeks.

As for the science of theology (al-kalām), its material is the discrimination between demonstrations (barāhīn) and fallacies (aghālīṭ), the discrimination between [genuine] sciences and [mere] beliefs, and the discrimination between the courses of the intellects and their stopping-points. As for its purpose, it is the encompassing comprehension of the origination of the world (ḥudūth al-ʿālam) and its neediness for an effective Maker (ṣāniʿ muʾaththir), qualified with what is necessary of the attributes, transcendent above what is impossible to conceive as an attribute of the Essence, powerful over the sending of the Messengers and the supporting of them with miracles.

As for the principles (al-uṣūl), its material is theology, jurisprudence, and language. The aspect of its derivation from theology is that the encompassing comprehension of the evidences erected upon the rulings is founded upon the acceptance of the revealed laws (al-sharāʾiʿ) and the verification of the Messengers — and there is no aspiration to that except after knowledge of the Sender (al-mursil). The aspect of its derivation from jurisprudence is that jurisprudence is the signified (al-madlūl), and the pursuit of the evidence while being heedless of the signified is a thing repudiated by the pathways of the intellects. The aspect of its derivation from language is that the uṣūlī (legal theorist) is driven to discourse concerning the import of the address (faḥwā al-khiṭāb), the interpretation (taʾwīl) of the reports of the Messenger — peace be upon him — and the explicit texts (nuṣūṣ) of the Book.

And its purpose is the knowledge of the definitive evidences (al-adillah al-qaṭʿiyyah) erected upon the prescriptive rulings (al-aḥkām al-taklīfiyyah), the solitary reports (akhbār al-āḥād), the pathways of inference (masālik al-ʿibar), and the analogies (maqāyīs) and the elicited [principles] (al-mustathārah). The [evidences] adduced by way of independent reasoning (ijtihād) are not of the principles — for they are matters of conjecture (ẓanniyyāt) taken in the manner of certainties — but the uṣūlī is nevertheless compelled to mention them in order to make clear the sound from the corrupt, and the well-grounded from the deviant; and because the weighings of preponderance (al-tarjīḥāt) are among the most obscure matters of the science of principles, and there is no way to them except by the elucidation of the ranks and degrees.

As for jurisprudence (al-fiqh), its material is the principles, and its purpose is the knowledge of the legal rulings (al-aḥkām al-sharʿiyyah) and the establishment of the rulings — when the conjectural indicators (al-ʿalāmāt al-maẓnūnah) appear — as known through definitive evidences, with no conjecture therein.

### Section

There is no science among these sciences except that it has loci of consensus (mawāqiʿ ijmāʿ) and sources of dispute (mathārāt nizāʿ). The locus of consensus in theology is the things perceived by primary necessity (al-mudrakāt bil-bidāyah), the necessary truths (al-ḍarūriyyāt), and the intelligibles (al-maʿqūlāt) in which the direction of inquiry is unified and does not multiply — like the consensus of the rational ones that the eternal (al-qadīm) does not pass away. The source of disagreement therein is the conflict of evidences and ambiguities (taʿāruḍ al-adillah wal-shubuhāt).

As for the science of principles, the origin of agreement therein resembles the origin of agreement in theology; and the spring of disagreement therein is two things: one of them is the conflict of evidences and ambiguities, and the second is the intermingling of the definitive (qaṭʿī) with the conjectural (ẓannī) within it.

As for jurisprudence, the locus of consensus therein is what is grounded in the text (naṣṣ) of the Book of God, or an unbrokenly transmitted report (ḥadīth mutawātir), or a consensus (ijmāʿ) obligatory to follow. Whatever is beyond that belongs to the loci of conjectures (maẓān al-ẓunūn); and when confusion arises therein, the mujtahids differ and their opinions fluctuate, and they split into factions.

chapters.title_en: Section on the Discussion of Legal Rulings (Al-Aḥkām al-Sharʿiyyah)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | باب القول في الأحكام الشرعية

ليست أحكام الأفعال صفات ذاتية وإنما معناها ارتباط خطاب الشارع بها نهيا
وأمرا وحثا وزجرا فالمحرم هو المقول فيه لا تفعلوه والواجب هو المقول فيه
لا تتركوه وهو كالنبوة ليست صفة ذاتية للنبي ولكنها عبارة عن اختصاص شخص
بتبليغ خطاب الشارع فقولنا الخمر محرمة تجوز فإنها جماد لا يتعلق بها
الخطاب وإنما المحرم تناولها مسألة لا يستدرك حسن الأفعال وقبحا بمسالك
العقول بل يتوقف دركها على الشرع المنقول
فالحسن عندنا ما حسنه الشرع بالحث عليه والقبيح ما قبحه بالزجر عنه والذم
عليه وقد خالف في ذلك المعتزلة والكرامية والروافض فقالوا الحسن حسن لذاته
والقبيح كذلك ثم قسموا ذلك إلى ما يستدرك بمحض العقل والى ما لا يستدرك إلا
بانضمام الشرع إليه كحسن الزكوات والصلوات وأنواع العبادات لأن مصالحهما
الخفية لا يطلع عليها إلا بتنبيه وما يستدرك بمحض العقل على زعمهم ينقسم
إلى
المعلوم بضرورة العقل عندهم كحسن الشكر وانقاذ الغرقى والهلكى وكقبح
الايلام ابتداء أو الكذب الذي لا غرض فيه
والى المعلوم بالنظر كالكذب الذي يرتبط به غرض ولنا في هذه المسألة
مسلكان أحدهما ابطال مذهبهم والثاني اثبات مذهب أهل الحق ولنا في ابطال
مذهبهم طريقتان إحداهما جدلية والأخرى معنوية أما الطريقة الجدلية فهي أنا
نقول ادعيتم أن حسن بعض الأفعال وقبحها مستدرك ببداية العقول  واوائلها ونحن
ننازعكم في ذلك ومواضع الضرورات لا يتصور فيها الخلاف بين العقلاء فإن
نسبونا إلى عناد عكسنا عليهم دعواهم ثم العناد إنما يتصور في شرذمة يسيرة
ونحن الجم الغفير والجمع الكبير لا يتصور منا التواطؤ على
كر العصور وتوالي الدهور من غير فرض رجوع من واحد إلى الانصاف وقولكم
أنكم وافقتمونا على اصل العلم وخالفتمونا من في مسندة اهو العقل أم الشرع
وذلك لا يمنع دعوي الضرورة كمخالفتكم في الكعبي في علم التواتر في كونه
نظريا قلنا ايلام الله سبحانه البهائم معلوم عندكم قبحه بالضرورة لو لم
يقدر تعويض ونحن ننازعكم في نفس هذا العلم مع اعتقاد نفي التعويض وبطلان
مذهب التناسخية
ثم نحن لا نسلم لكم لحسن الراجع إلى الذات وانما المعني بالحسن عندنا ما
يحسنه الشارع بالحث عليه ولو قدر عدم ورود الشرع لضاهي بن الكفر الإيمان
عندنا فكيف يستقيم ادعاؤكم الموافقة في أصل العلم واما الطريقة المعنوية
فهي أنا نقول ما قولكم في واقف على فوهة طريق اجتاز به نبي واشياعه واتبعه
غاشم يبغي قتله واستخبره هذه عن حاله ايصدق سنة أم يكذب فإن صدق فهو سعي في
روح نبي وان كذب فهو مستقبح لذاته عندكم وصفات الذات لا تتبدل ونحن نعلم إن
الكذب احسن من الصدق ههنا المسلك الثاني في اثبات المذهب نقول القتل الواقع
اعتداء يجانس القتل المستوفى قصاصا في الصورة والصفات بدليل إن الفافل عمرو
عن المستند فيهما لا يميز بينهما والمختلفان في صفة الذات يستحيل اشتباههما
وتجانسهما وكذا الوطء في النكاح والزنا فآل مأخذهما إلى
الاغراض جلبا ودفعا ونحن لا ننكر تفاوت الافعال عند العقلاء لتفاوت
الاغراض وانما الخلاف في الافعال بالنسبة إلى الله تعالى وهو منزه عن
الاغراض لا يتضرر بالكفر ولا ينتفع بالايمان فلا معنى للتمييز في حقه وكذا
فعله تعالى لا يطلب له غرض فيه حتى إذا خالف غرضه قبح ولا تحكم للعباد عليه
وهو يفعل ما يشاء فلا يجب عليه تطبيق افعاله على غرض العباد وهو متصرف في
ملكه لا اعتراض عليه اصلا ولهم أربع شبه احدها انهم قالوا استحسان مكارم
الاخلاق من الشكر والإحسان وانقاذ
الغرقى والهلكى واستقباح الكذب والايلام اطبق عليه العقلاء مع تفاوت
قرائحهم فدل على انه مدرك بالضرورة قلنا نعم ذلك مسلم فيما بين الناس ومنشؤ
اغراضهم والكفر كالايمان بالنسبة إلى الله عز وجل وليس كالكفر والشكر
بالنسبة إلينا فإنا
نفرح ونرتاح بالشكر ونغتم قبل بالكفران وسر العبودية التلفت إلى الحظوظ
حتى لو ورد الأمر المجرد من الشارع من غير عقاب لما قضى العقل بامتثاله إذ
لا غرض لنا ولا للرب سبحانه فيه فإذا اورد العقاب قضى العقل باجتنابه وسر
الربوبية! التنزة يحيى عن الحظوظ ومن لم ينزه فقد ذهل عن حقيقة الالهية
الثانية إن قالوا ما بال الملك العظيم الولي على الاقاليم يحسن إلى فقير
وان اشرف على الموت من غير توقع غرض فيه ليس ذلك إلا لتحسين العقل قلنا
المستحث عليه أما استمرار العادة وهي طبيعة خاصة يعسر خلافها أو رقة
الجنسية والرب تعالى منزه عن الرقة والشفقة الثالثة انهم قالوا إن البراهمة
ونفاة الشرائع ادركوا الحسن والقبح ولا مستند لهم إلا محض العقل قلنا ذلك
اعتقاد فاسد كاعتقادكم الرحمن وليس ذلك بعلم كإحالتهم وكان بعثة الرسل
الرابعة
قولهم إن العاقل يؤثر الصدق على الكذب عند استوائهما في الافضاء إلى
الغرض وسببه تحسين العقل قلنا لا بل سببه الشرع أو حذر اللوم من الناس أو
تقليد مذهبهم الفاسد فإن فرضوا عدم هذه المعاني فيستوي عنده الصدق والكذب
ثم غايتهم اعتبار الغائب بالشاهد ويقبح من السيد شاهدا إن يترك عبيده
واماءه يموج بعضهم في بعض يزنون ويقتحمون الفواحش وهو قادر على منعهم وقد
فعله الرب سبحانه والخلائق في قبضته وقهره فإن قيل تركهم لينزجروا بأنفسهم
مؤثرين فيستحقون الثواب قلنا وقد علم انهم لا يفعلون فليمنعهم اجبارا وكم
من مجبر ممنوع بزمانة أو عجز عن ارتكاب الفواحش
مسألة لا يستدرك وجوب شكر المنعم بالعقل خلافا للمعتزلة لان العقل
لا يوجب الشئ هزلا هملا فلا  بد من تخيل غرض وذلك يستحيل رجوعه إلى
المشكور فإنه تعالى منزه عن الأغراض والشاكر أيضا لا يلتذ به في الحال بل
يتعب نفسه فإن قيل يعرض له انه إن شكر ربه بعد أن عرفه اثيب فيثاب وان كفر
فربما يعاقب فعقله يستحثه على سلوك طريق الأمن كالمسافر إذا تصدى له طريقان
على هذا الوجه قلنا توقع العقاب مختصا بجانب الكفر خيال فاسد مستنده تخيل
غرض في الشكر والمعرفة وهما متساويان عند الرب فلا تمييز
ثم نقول وقد يخطر للعبد انه إن نظر وشكر ربما يعاقب فإنه عبد مرفه أمده
الله تعالى بأسباب التنعم فلعله خلقه للترفه فإتعابه نفسه تصرف منه في
مملكته من غير اذنه ولهم شبهتان إحداهما ادعاؤهم اطباق العقلاء على استحسان
الشكر واستقباح الكفران وذلك مسلم فيما يرجع إلى الناس لانهم يهتزون بالشكر
ويغتمون بالكفر والرب تعالى يستوي في حقه الامران ويعضد هذا الكلام شيئان
أحدهما إن المتقرب إلى السلطان بتحريك انملته في زاوية حجرته يسفه في عقله
وعبادات العباد بالنسبة إلى جلال الله دونه في الرتبة والثاني إن من تصدق
عليه السطان بكسرة من رغيف في غير مخمصة فلو أخذ يدور في البلاد وينادي على
رؤوس الاشهاد يشكره كان
ذلك خزيا وافتضاحا وجملة انعام الله تعالى على عباده بالنسبة إلى
مقدوراته دون ذلك بالنسبة إلى السلطان الثانية قولهم حصر مدارك الوجوب في
الشرع المنقول دون مسالك العقول يؤدي إلى افحام الرسول فإنه إذا اظهر
المعجزة ودعا الناس إلى النظر قالوا لا يجب علينا النظر في معجزاتك إلا

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ك-م (ḥ-k-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of judgment, governance, and decisive authority; a ruling that settles a matter.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The divine address (khiṭāb) as the source of legal valuation; rulings are relational, not intrinsic.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — the ruling is a real attribute of the divine command, not of the act itself; applying it to the act is metaphorical (majāz).
- Root: ح-س-ن (ḥ-s-n) and ق-ب-ح (q-b-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Beauty and ugliness as perceptual qualities.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, these are not intrinsic to acts but determined by divine commendation (ḥathth) and deterrence (zajr).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The literal sense is sensory; the legal sense is a transferred (majāzī) application.
- Root: ك-ل-ف (k-l-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Burden, toil, and hardship.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Taklīf is the imposition of a duty involving difficulty; its validity requires capacity (qudrah) and comprehension (fahm).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — loading a burden; metaphorical — legal obligation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The structure "al-muḥarram huwa al-maqūl fīhi lā tafʿalūh" employs a nominal sentence with a pronominal referent, clarifying that the predicate defines the subject through the divine address, not through inherent attributes.
chapters.translation:
I say: The rulings concerning acts are not intrinsic attributes (ṣifāt dhātiyyah) of those acts. Rather, their meaning is the connection of the Lawgiver's address (khiṭāb al-shāriʿ) to them — as prohibition (nahy), command (amr), urging (ḥathth), and deterrence (zajr). Thus, the forbidden (al-muḥarram) is that concerning which it is said, "Do not do it," and the obligatory (al-wājib) is that concerning which it is said, "Do not abandon it." This is like prophethood (nubuwwah): it is not an intrinsic attribute of the prophet, but rather an expression of a person's being singled out for conveying the Lawgiver's address. Therefore, our saying "wine is forbidden" is a metaphorical expression (tajawwuz), for wine is an inanimate object to which the address does not attach; rather, what is forbidden is its consumption.

A Question: The goodness (ḥusn) and badness (qubḥ) of acts are not apprehended through the pathways of the intellects (masālik al-ʿuqūl); rather, their apprehension depends on the transmitted Law (al-sharʿ al-manqūl). Thus, in our view, the good (al-ḥasan) is what the Law has deemed good by urging toward it, and the bad (al-qabīḥ) is what the Law has deemed bad by deterring from it and censuring it. The Muʿtazilah, the Karrāmiyyah, and the Rāfiḍah have opposed us in this, saying: "The good is good in itself, and the bad is likewise." They then divided this into what is apprehended by pure reason and what is not apprehended except by the addition of the Law to it — such as the goodness of alms (zakāt), prayers (ṣalawāt), and the various acts of worship, because their hidden interests (maṣāliḥ) are not known except through divine notification. What is apprehended by pure reason, on their claim, divides into: (1) what is known by the necessity of reason (ḍarūrat al-ʿaql) — such as the goodness of gratitude (shukr), rescuing the drowning and the perishing, and the badness of causing pain (īlām) initially, or lying that serves no purpose; and (2) what is known by reflection (naẓar) — such as lying connected to some purpose.

We have two pathways (maslakān) in this matter: one is the refutation of their doctrine, and the second is the establishment of the doctrine of the people of truth (ahl al-ḥaqq). For refuting their doctrine, we have two methods: one is dialectical (jadalī), and the other is substantive (maʿnawī).

As for the dialectical method: We say — you have claimed that the goodness and badness of some acts are apprehended by the beginnings and first principles of intellects (badāyā al-ʿuqūl wa-awāʾiluhā). We dispute this with you. The loci of necessities (ḍarūrāt) admit no disagreement among the rational. If you attribute our position to obstinacy (ʿinād), we reverse your claim upon you. Moreover, obstinacy is only conceivable in a small faction, whereas we are the great multitude (al-jamm al-ghafīr); it is inconceivable that we would collude upon falsehood across the succession of ages and the passage of times, without supposing that a single one of us would return to fairness. As for your saying, "You have agreed with us on the principle of knowledge (aṣl al-ʿilm) but disagreed with us only regarding its basis — whether it is reason or the Law" — this does not prevent our claim of necessity, just as you have disagreed with al-Kaʿbī regarding the knowledge of successive transmission (tawātur) in that he deemed it theoretical. We say: The infliction of pain by God upon beasts — you hold its badness to be known by necessity, if no compensation (ʿiwaḍ) is supposed. Yet we dispute with you regarding this very knowledge itself, while affirming the negation of compensation and the falsity of the doctrine of transmigration (tanāsukh).

Furthermore, we do not concede to you the goodness that reverts to the essence (al-ḥusn al-rājiʿ ilā al-dhāt). Rather, by "good" in our view is meant what the Lawgiver deems good by urging toward it. Even if we suppose the non-arrival of the Law, then in our view disbelief (kufr) would resemble faith (īmān) — so how can your claim of agreement with us on the principle of knowledge stand?

As for the substantive method: We say — what do you say about a person standing at the head of a road, when a prophet and his followers pass by, and a tyrant (ghāshim) seeking to kill him follows them, and the tyrant asks this person about the prophet's condition — should he tell the truth or lie? If he tells the truth, he has striven toward the destruction of a prophet's life; if he lies, then it is deemed bad in itself (mustaqbaḥ li-dhātihi) in your view. But attributes of the essence do not change. We know with certainty that lying is better than truthfulness in this situation.

The second pathway — in establishing the doctrine: We say — the killing that occurs as aggression (iʿtidāʾ) is homogeneous with the killing exacted as retaliation (qiṣāṣ) in form and attributes, as evidenced by the fact that a heedless observer, ignorant of the underlying basis, cannot distinguish between them. Two things that differ in an essential attribute cannot possibly be confused with each other or be homogeneous. Likewise, sexual intercourse in marriage (nikāḥ) and in fornication (zinā) — so their bases revert to purposes (aghrāḍ), whether for attainment (jalb) or repulsion (dafʿ). We do not deny that acts differ among the rational due to differing purposes. Rather, the disagreement concerns acts in relation to God Most High — and He is exalted above purposes (munazzah ʿan al-aghrāḍ). He is not harmed by disbelief nor benefited by faith, so there is no meaning to differentiation in His regard. Likewise, His act — no purpose is sought in it, such that if it contradicted His purpose it would be deemed bad. No judgment of servants applies over Him; He does what He wills. It is not incumbent upon Him to conform His acts to the purposes of His servants. He disposes of His dominion (mulk); no objection applies to Him at all.

They have four dubious arguments (shubah):

First: They said — the approval of noble character traits (makārim al-akhlāq) — such as gratitude, beneficence, and rescuing the drowning and perishing — and the disapproval of lying and causing pain — the rational have unanimously agreed upon these despite the divergence of their natural faculties. This indicates that it is apprehended by necessity. We say: Yes, this is conceded among people, and its source is their purposes. But disbelief is like faith in relation to God, Mighty and Majestic — not like disbelief and gratitude in relation to us. For we rejoice and take comfort in gratitude, and we grieve over ingratitude. The secret of servitude (sirr al-ʿubūdiyyah) is attention to one's shares (iltifāt ilā al-ḥuẓūẓ). Even if a bare command came from the Lawgiver without punishment, reason would not decree obedience to it, since there is no purpose for us nor for the Lord in it. But when punishment is introduced, reason decrees avoidance of it. The secret of lordship (sirr al-rubūbiyyah) is transcendence (tanzīh) above shares. Whoever does not deem Him transcendent has been heedless of the reality of divinity (ḥaqīqat al-ilāhiyyah).

Second: If they say — how is it that a great king, a guardian over provinces, does good to a poor person on the verge of death, without expecting any purpose in it? This is only due to reason's approval. We say: What urges him is either the continuation of habit (istimrār al-ʿādah) — which is a particular nature whose contravention is difficult — or the tenderness of shared species (riqqat al-jinsiyyah). The Lord is exalted above tenderness and compassion (al-riqqah wa-al-shafaqah).

Third: They said — the Brahmins (Barāhimah) and the deniers of religious laws apprehended goodness and badness, and they have no basis except pure reason. We say: That is a corrupt belief (iʿtiqād fāsid), like your belief in the Most Merciful — and it is not knowledge, just as their denial of the sending of messengers is not knowledge.

Fourth: Their saying — the rational person prefers truthfulness over lying when both lead equally to the same purpose, and the cause of this is reason's approval. We say: No — rather, its cause is the Law, or fear of people's blame, or imitation (taqlīd) of their corrupt doctrine. If these meanings are supposed absent, then truthfulness and lying become equal to him.

Then their ultimate resort is to analogize the unseen to the witnessed (qiyās al-ghāʾib ʿalā al-shāhid): It is deemed bad of a master, in the witnessed world, to leave his male and female slaves surging into one another, fornicating and plunging into obscenities, while he is able to prevent them. Yet the Lord has done this — and all creatures are in His grasp and His subjugation. If it is said: "He left them so that they might restrain themselves by their own choice, thereby deserving reward" — we say: He knows they will not do so, so let Him prevent them by force. How many are forcibly prevented by chronic illness (zamānah) or incapacity from committing obscenities!

A Question: The obligation of gratitude to the Benefactor (wujūb shukr al-munʿim) is not apprehended by reason — contrary to the Muʿtazilah — because reason does not necessitate anything frivolously or negligently. A purpose must be imagined, and that is impossible to revert to the one thanked, for He is exalted above purposes. Nor does the one thanking derive pleasure from it in the present moment; rather, he wearies himself. If it is said: "It occurs to him that if he thanks his Lord after knowing Him, he will be rewarded, and if he disbelieves, he may be punished — so his reason urges him to take the path of safety, like a traveler who faces two roads in this manner" — we say: The expectation of punishment being specific to the side of disbelief is a corrupt imagination (khayāl fāsid), whose basis is imagining a purpose in gratitude and knowledge — and these two are equal in the Lord's regard, so there is no differentiation.

Then we say: It may also occur to the servant that if he reflects and gives thanks, he might be punished — for he is a pampered servant whom God has supplied with the means of comfort; perhaps He created him for indulgence, so wearying himself is an act of disposal in His dominion without His permission.

They have two dubious arguments:

First: Their claim of the rational consensus on approving gratitude and disapproving ingratitude. This is conceded regarding what reverts to people, for they are stirred by gratitude and grieved by ingratitude — but the Lord holds both matters equal. Two things support this statement: (1) One who seeks nearness to a sultan by moving his fingertip in the corner of his chamber is deemed foolish by his own intellect — and the acts of servants relative to the majesty of God are lower in rank than this. (2) If a sultan gave someone a crumb of bread in charity when not in dire hunger, and that person then went about the lands proclaiming his thanks at the heads of assemblies — that would be disgrace and humiliation. The totality of God's blessings upon His servants, relative to His capacities, is far below this relative to a sultan.

Second: Their saying — confining the avenues of obligation (madārik al-wujūb) to the transmitted Law rather than the pathways of intellects leads to silencing the Messenger (ifḥām al-rasūl). For when he displays a miracle and calls people to reflection, they say: "Reflection upon your miracles is not obligatory upon us except by an established Law — so establish your Law first, that we may then reflect upon your miracle." The answer is from two aspects:

First: This also applies to you, because reason by its very essence does not indicate obligation — for if it did, no rational person would ever be free of knowledge of every intelligible. Yet a rational person may see a miracle and be heedless of it, not reflecting until the obligation of reflection becomes evident. Their saying that "a person is never free of two thoughts" is an imposition upon sense-perception (ijtirāʾ ʿalā al-ḥiss) — and it is more fitting that he recall this at the appearance of the miracle, not before. Its obligation is not, in your view, specific to the arrival of the Law. Moreover, he may disdain the Messenger, giving him no weight, and persist in his heedlessness — as we see in those who attend preaching assemblies and remain immersed in heedlessness while the preacher exhorts them atop the pulpits with cries.

The second answer — and it is the verified one (al-taḥqīq): Obligation is established by the establishment of the Law. So when the miracle appears, the Law is established — this does not depend on any acceptor's acceptance. And obligation (taklīf) requires only possibility (imkān), which has been realized. If he is granted success, he succeeds; otherwise, he perishes. Concerning this it was said: One does not draw near to God through the first act of reflection (awwal naẓar), for he does not know it — since if he knew it, he would know it through another reflection, and the first would cease to be first.

A Question: There is no ruling before the arrival of the Law (lā ḥukm qabla wurūd al-sharʿ). It is transmitted from some that acts are prohibited (maḥẓūrah) before the arrival of the Law, and from others that they are permissible (mubāḥah). One should not suppose of the prohibitionists that they imagined prohibition in what the intellects deem good, nor in what the soul cannot do without — such as eating and drinking. Nor should one suppose of the permissivists that they deemed permissible what reason deems bad — such as causing pain and lying. Perhaps they said this regarding matters in which reason does not judge goodness or badness. We say: The judgment of prohibition is an arbitrary imposition (taḥakkum) not apprehended by rational reflection nor by necessity, since no purpose of deterrence attaches to it, nor can it be estimated in acts of commission. As for permissibility (ibāḥah): if they mean by it the equivalence of abstention and commission with the negation of rulings — that is the wished-for thing. But if they claim that permissibility is a ruling, then a ruling of God is His address — so who is the conveyer, when there is no messenger?

The Discussion of Obligatory Rulings (al-Aḥkām al-Taklīfiyyah): Taklīf is derived from kulfah (burden) on the pattern of tafʿīl. Its meaning is the imposition of that in whose doing there is hardship (mashaqqah). Under it are included obligation (ījāb) and prohibition (ḥaẓr) — whether the act is what nature yearns toward or recoils from. As for recommendation (nadb): according to al-Qāḍī, it is part of taklīf, because specifying an act with the promise of reward urges the rational person toward it — and this is a form of burden. The chosen view (al-mukhtār) is that it is not part of taklīf, because it came with the lifting of restriction (rafʿ al-janāḥ). Permissibility (ibāḥah) is not part of taklīf except according to the master Abū Isḥāq. He said: "The aspect of burden is the obligation to believe that it is legally permissible." This is weak, for that is derived from affirming the messengers, and the act itself involves no burden.

The detailed discussion of obligations is encompassed by four questions:

Question 1: Our master Abū al-Ḥasan (al-Ashʿarī) — may God have mercy on him — held the permissibility of obligating what cannot be borne (taklīf mā lā yuṭāq), adducing His saying: {«wa-lā tuḥammilnā mā lā ṭāqata lanā bih»} ("And do not burden us with what we cannot bear") — and there is no point to supplication unless that is conceivable in the mind. He also adduced that Abū Jahl was obligated to affirm the truthfulness of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) after the Messenger's tongue had conveyed that he would not affirm — so the sum of it is obligating him to affirm that he will not affirm. This doctrine befits the doctrine of our master Abū al-Ḥasan and is entailed by it in two aspects: (1) In his view, the originated power (al-qudrah al-ḥādithah) has no effect upon the empowered act (al-maqdūr); it occurs by God's invention (ikhtirāʿ), and we have been obligated with the act of another. (2) In his view, the one sitting is not capable of standing, yet he is commanded to stand, and the power to stand accompanies the standing itself. The saying of some of our companions — "Sitting is within his power, so he is commanded to abandon it" — does not rescue from this, for the command is directed at standing, which is not within his power. If the one sitting is commanded to fly, he has been commanded with what he absolutely cannot bear, even if he is able to abandon sitting.

The chosen view in our doctrine is the impossibility of obligating what cannot be borne (istihālat taklīf mā lā yuṭāq). Yes, the imperative form may be issued for incapacitation (taʿjīz) — as in His saying: {«kūnū qiradatan khāsiʾīn»} ("Be apes, despised") — and for informing of power — as in His saying: {«kun fa-yakūn»} ("Be, and it is") — and it is not issued for address and request. This is like His saying: {«ḥattā yalija al-jamalu fī sammi al-khiyāṭ»} ("until the camel passes through the eye of the needle") — its meaning is remoteness, not what is understood from the form of conditionality. For it is impossible to request of the obligated what he cannot bear.

The proof of its impossibility: A command is a request attached to a requested object (maṭlūb), just as knowledge is attached to a known object. The combination of standing and sitting is not intelligible, so it cannot be a requested object, and requesting it is impossible, since it is not intelligible in itself.

Our chosen view is that the originated power has a connection to the empowered act, and capacity (istiṭāʿah) — even if it accompanies the act — yet in the Law nothing is obligated except what one can definitively accomplish. This is evident in the sources and channels of the Law, and in its promise and threat — for there is no meaning to singling out one agent's act over another's for punishment or reward while all are equal in incapacity regarding it. This is something impossible. The ruling on capacity is mentioned in theology (al-kalām).

As for Abū Jahl: he was obligated to say "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God" — and he was capable of it. Then the Lord informed that he would refrain — out of obstinacy, despite capacity — and the Messenger conveyed this as He knew it.

If it is said: "The disbelievers who did not believe were obligated with faith, and He knew they would not believe — and the contrary of the known is inconceivable to occur, so this was obligating what cannot be borne" — we say: This reverses upon the one who imposes it regarding the contrary of the known in God's regard, for it is possible by agreement, even if it did not occur. The verification (al-taḥqīq): What is possible in itself is permissible of occurrence; its reality is not changed by knowledge. God empowered the disbelievers over faith, then knew they would refrain despite capacity — so it was as He knew. The possible did not turn into impossible because He informed us of it through His knowledge.

Question 2: The intoxicated person (al-sakrān) is not obligated, because the condition of address is comprehension (fahm), and he is deprived of it. The intoxicated person does not understand. If it is said to him, "Understand," that would be obligating what cannot be borne. The jurists (fuqahāʾ) held that he is addressed, clinging to His saying: {«lā taqrabū al-ṣalāta wa-antum sukārā»} ("Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated"). But the apparent meaning of the verse does not clash with the intelligibles. Moreover, it is an address to the slightly tipsy (al-muntashī) whose intellect has not departed — as evidenced by the fact that it was revealed concerning a wine-drinker who led a people in prayer and recited the Fātiḥah, then "Say: O disbelievers" became confused upon him — yet he had enough intellect to understand. His saying: {«ḥattā taʿlamū mā taqūlūn»} ("until you know what you say") means "so that you may be in full certainty." They may also cling to the obligation of making up prayers (qaḍāʾ) and the effectiveness of divorce (ṭalāq) and the totality of rulings. We say: The application of rulings to him is a severity (taghlīẓ), because intoxication is yearned for by souls, and he has transgressed by causing himself to reach it — so the address is not directed to him during intoxication at all. The rulings apply, and the prayer is made up by a new command. If a madman after recovery, or a menstruating woman after purity, were commanded with the act of fasting, that would not be remote — and its cause is his transgression by causing himself to reach it, despite his being mad. Even if he threw himself from a precipice and his feet were dislocated, no make-up would be obligatory, because the soul does not yearn toward it. The disagreement reverts to an expression: if they concede to us the impossibility of obligating what cannot be borne, then we concede the rulings and their application — but that does not indicate obligation. The intoxicated person does not understand, and it is not said to him, "Understand" — and that is the condition of every address. Likewise, the forgetful and heedless person: his ruling is the ruling of the intoxicated regarding obligation.

Question 3: The disbelievers are addressed by the branches of the Law (furūʿ al-sharīʿah) — according to al-Shāfiʿī, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah. The proof of the permissibility of obligating them with the branches: reason does not deem it impossible, since reaching it through the prior establishment of faith is possible — just as the person in minor impurity (muḥdith) is addressed with prayer on the condition of prior purification, and just as they conceded to us that the one who denies the Creator (muʿaṭṭil) is addressed with affirming the Messenger (peace be upon him) on the condition of prior knowledge of the messengers. This is a proof of permissibility. As for its actual occurrence (wuqūʿ), it is definitively established in our view. Al-Qāḍī wavered on whether it is definitive or probable. We know with certainty that the Messenger (peace be upon him) was sent to the strata of creatures, and they were obligated to accept his Law, generation after generation, in its principles and details — even if reaching it is contingent upon faith, like prayer in the case of the one in minor impurity and the one who denies the Creator. The secret of the matter: the disbeliever is not addressed with the prayer itself along with disbelief, but he is commanded with it in the manner of reaching it (ʿalā wajh al-tawassul). We say the same regarding the one in minor impurity. It is reported from Abū Hāshim that the one in minor impurity is not addressed with prayer — and this was attributed to breaching consensus (kharq al-ijmāʿ). If he meant what we have mentioned, it is true; if he meant that he is not punished for abandoning prayer, it is false.

Question 4: The one compelled (al-mukrah) to a thing — it is permissible that he be addressed with it, contrary to the Muʿtazilah. For his choice (ikhtiyār) remains, and he is able to proceed. The condition of obligation is the ability to comply (tamakkun min al-imtithāl). The evidence of the persistence of his choice is his deliberation between proceeding and abstaining. They say: His nature (jibillah) urges him to the act to save his life — so it is the cause of his proceeding, not the intention of compliance (qaṣd al-imtithāl) — hence he deserves no reward for it, and it is deemed bad to command what one deserves no reward for. On this basis they said: It is deemed bad of the Lord, Glorified and Majestic, to manifest a sign to which necks bow and by which the masses of servants believe — because that involves no choice, so no command attaches to it. These principles are false in our view.

The limit of what makes obligation permissible in our view: what is not impossible in reason to occur, with the obligated person's ability to do it. Al-Qāḍī — may God be pleased with him — imposed upon them the sin of the one compelled to kill, and attributed them in this matter to breaching consensus. This is not entailed, for they say: It is not remote that he be commanded with restraint (inzijār) despite the compulsion of his nature — indeed, he is more deserving of reward, like ablution in severe cold and bearing hardships in acts of worship. And God knows best.
